## Simple explanation

A Jupyter Notebook is an interactive document where users can write and run
code in small sections called cells. Code, output, charts, and explanatory text
can live together in one file.

## Technical explanation

Notebook documents store an ordered collection of code, Markdown, and raw-text
cells along with outputs and metadata. A language kernel executes code cells
and returns results to the notebook interface. The standard `.ipynb` format is
JSON-based.

## Why it matters in AI engineering

Notebooks are useful for exploratory data analysis, visualization,
prototyping, and teaching machine-learning concepts. They make it easy to
inspect intermediate results, but production workflows often need to move
stable logic into tested modules or pipelines.

## How it works

The notebook interface sends code cells to a running kernel. The kernel
executes them in a persistent session and returns outputs such as text, tables,
or plots. Since the session retains variables, the order in which cells are
executed can differ from their displayed order.

## Practical example

A data scientist can load a dataset in one cell, inspect missing values in the
next, train a baseline model in another, and visualize evaluation metrics
alongside the code and notes explaining each decision.

## Common misconceptions

- Cell order in the file does not guarantee execution order in a live session.
- A notebook that works in one environment may fail elsewhere if dependencies,
  data files, or random seeds are not documented.
- Notebooks are useful for exploration, but they do not automatically provide
  production-grade testing or deployment.
